scenes.heading: Completing the square
scenes.say: How can x squared plus six x plus five be written as x plus three, all squared, minus four? In this video you'll learn to complete the square, and use it to find minimum values and factorise tricky quadratics.
scenes.caption: How can x² + 6x + 5 be written as (x + 3)² − 4? In this video you'll learn to complete the square, and use it to find minimum values and factorise tricky quadratics.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: A square floor is missing its corner tile, so you borrow one
scenes.science: Add the missing corner to make a square, then subtract it again
scenes.breaks: Real tiles can't have a negative size, but the number left after paying back can be negative.
scenes.say: Imagine tiling a square floor, but the corner tile is missing. You borrow one from the shed to finish the square, but now you owe the shed a tile. Completing the square is the same: add the missing corner to make a perfect square, then subtract it again so nothing changes.

scenes.heading: The missing corner
scenes.say: Here is x squared plus six x. First the big square, x squared. Then six x split into two strips of three x. Now there's a gap in the corner, three by three, so its area is nine. Add the nine and you have a perfect square: x plus three, all squared.
scenes.caption: First the big square, x². Then 6x split into two strips of 3x. The gap in the corner is 3 by 3, area 9. Add it: x² + 6x + 9 = (x + 3)².

scenes.heading: Halve it, square it
scenes.say: Here's the method. Halve the coefficient of x. Square it. Add it and subtract it, so the value doesn't change. Then write the first three terms as a perfect square.

scenes.heading: Worked example
scenes.question: Write x² + 6x + 5 in completed-square form, then factorise.
scenes.say: Half of six is three, and three squared is nine. Add nine and take away nine. That gives x plus three, all squared, minus four. Four is two squared, so this is a difference of two squares. It factorises to x plus one, times x plus five.
scenes.caption: Half of 6 is 3, and 3² = 9. Add and subtract 9: (x + 3)² − 4. Since 4 = 2², it is a difference of two squares: (x + 1)(x + 5).

scenes.heading: Finding a minimum
scenes.question: Find the minimum value of x² − 12x + 40.
scenes.say: Find the smallest value of x squared minus twelve x plus forty. Half of negative twelve is negative six, and that squared is thirty-six. Completing the square gives x minus six, all squared, plus four. A square can't be negative, so the smallest it can be is zero, when x is six. So the minimum value is four.
scenes.caption: Half of −12 is −6, squared is 36. Completing the square gives (x − 6)² + 4. A square can't be negative, so the smallest is 0, when x = 6. Minimum value: 4.

points: Add it and take it away
(x + h)² + k: minimum k at x = −h
scenes.say: Quick recap. Halve the x coefficient and square it. Add it and take it away. The completed form tells you the minimum value, and if it's a square minus a number, you can factorise it using a square root. Now try the practice questions!
